warmup.q: In Kotlin, recipes.filter { it.vegan }.map { it.name } runs on a List. How many lambda objects does one call create?
options: None: filter and map are inline, so the lambda bodies are copied into plain loops
warmup.why: filter and map on Iterable are inline functions. The compiler pastes their loops, and the bodies of your lambdas, into the calling method, so no lambda object is ever created. The call still builds two new ArrayLists, one per step: that is the real cost of a chain, and the next lessons deal with it. Lesson 2's answer, one object per capturing lambda, applies to functions that are not inline. The last section shows the bytecode.

opening:
Picture a friend who is good in the kitchen. You hand them any recipe card, and they hand back a new card: "the same, but for six people", or "the same, but vegan", or "the same, and if it burns, try again". They don't need to know what the recipe makes. They change the card, not the dinner.

Code needs friends like that. Function types, lambdas and closures turned checks into values you can hold. The next step is a function whose arguments, or whose result, are such values. That sounds abstract until you notice the same loop copied around three calls, with one line changed each time.

The easy trap is to trust every such friend equally. One that "remembers last time's answer" is only right for recipes whose answer never changes, and it can't taste the difference.

In this lesson, we'll write retry and timed, return a function that is set up once, clip small functions together where order matters, build a memo that remembers, and see why inline makes Kotlin's own versions free. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a friend who takes any recipe card and hands back a new one. retry and timed took the work as a function, gramsFor handed back a converter set up once, andThen clipped small steps together in an order that matters, and memoize remembered answers, honestly only for pure functions.

Search your code for two loops that differ by one call, and for a fun that takes a lambda and calls it right away without inline. The first wants a higher-order function; the second wants one word.

Next, we'll put these functions to work on whole collections. What does a loop that builds four results at once look like without the loop?

sections.h: Passing in the part that changes: retry and timed take a function
sections.html:
Look at three places in a recipe app that call something flaky. A flaky call is one that fails now and then for reasons outside your code, like a website that is slow to answer and times out:

Java
// fetch a recipe page from the website
for (int attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    try { page = site.fetch("pancakes"); break; }
    catch (SiteTimeoutException e) { if (attempt == 3) throw e; }
}
// the same loop around shop.prices(basket)
// the same loop around weather.today()
Kotlin
// fetch a recipe page from the website
var attempt = 1
while (true) {
    try { page = site.fetch("pancakes"); break }
    catch (e: SiteTimeoutException) { if (attempt++ == 3) throw e }
}
// the same loop around shop.prices(basket)
// the same loop around weather.today()

The three loops are identical except for one call. An ordinary helper method can't pull that call out, because a method's parameters are values, and the call has to happen inside the loop, up to three times. What you need to pass in is the work itself.

A higher-order function is a function that takes a function as a parameter, returns one, or both. It's the friend from the opening: hand it a card, and it does something with the card. Here is retry written as one:

Java
static <T> T retry(int times, Supplier<T> block) {
    RuntimeException last = null;
    for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= times; attempt++) {
        try { return block.get(); }
        catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; }
    }
    throw new IllegalStateException("gave up after " + times + " attempts", last);
}

String page = retry(3, () -> site.fetch("pancakes"));
Kotlin
fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: () -> T): T {
    var last: Exception? = null
    repeat(times) {
        try { return block() } catch (e: Exception) { last = e }
    }
    throw IllegalStateException("gave up after $times attempts", last)
}

val page = retry(3) { site.fetch("pancakes") }

The loop is written once. The part that varies, the call, arrives as block, and retry decides when and how often to run it. That's the whole idea of this lesson: keep the shape of a computation (retry it, time it, remember it) apart from the work inside it. (The return inside repeat leaves retry itself. That only works because repeat is inline, which the last section explains.)

The demo's fake website times out twice, then answers. It also wraps the call in timed, a second higher-order function that runs any block and reports how long it took:

  attempt 1 failed: site timeout on call 1
  attempt 2 failed: site timeout on call 2
  fetch with retry took 41.14 ms
result: page:pancakes after 3 calls

Three calls, one page, and neither function knows what a recipe is. (The 41 ms is from a busy machine, and most of it is the JVM running brand-new code for the first time.)

Kotlin makes the call site read like a language feature. When the last parameter is a function, you can write the lambda after the parentheses. That's a trailing lambda, and if it's the only argument, you drop the parentheses too: retry(3) { ... }, timed("fetch") { ... }. That's why repeat, synchronized, use and buildList look built in. They're ordinary library functions.

Java needs an interface for the parameter, and checked exceptions get in the way. Those are exceptions the compiler makes you catch or declare, like IOException. Supplier.get() can't throw one, so retrying file or network code needs a Callable<T> and a throws Exception on retry. Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so () -> T fits every call.

When code differs by one call, pass the call in. Write the loop once.

That's functions in. The friend can also hand back a new card.

try.title: One retry loop for every flaky call
steps: Run Retry (or RetryJava). Predict first: how many calls reach the website in each half?
Wrap the second retry in timed("gave up") { ... } as well. Predict whether its timing line prints, even though the block throws.
Change the first retry(3) to retry(1) and run again.

code.title: Retry.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo // A fake recipe website that times out a few times, then answers. class FlakySite(private var failuresLeft: Int) { var calls = 0 fun fetch(recipe: String): String { calls++ if (failuresLeft-- > 0) throw IllegalStateException("site timeout on call $calls") return "page:$recipe" } } // A higher-order function: the loop is written once, and the work comes in as a function. fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: () -> T): T { var last: Exception? = null repeat(times) { attempt -> try { return block() // returns from retry: repeat is inline } catch (e: Exception) { last = e println(" attempt ${attempt + 1} failed: ${e.message}") } } throw IllegalStateException("gave up after $times attempts", last) } // Another one: run any block, report how long it took, hand back its result unchanged. fun <T> timed(label: String, block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return block() } finally { println(" $label took %.2f ms".format((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e6)) } } fun main() { val site = FlakySite(failuresLeft = 2) val page = timed("fetch with retry") { retry(3) { site.fetch("pancakes") } } println("result: $page after ${site.calls} calls") val down = FlakySite(failuresLeft = 5) try { retry(3) { down.fetch("waffles") } } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("result: ${e.message} (last cause: ${e.cause?.message})") } }

alt.title: RetryJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo; import java.util.function.Supplier; /** * Java twin of Retry.kt. The work comes in as a Supplier<T>. Supplier.get() can't throw checked * exceptions, so code that throws IOException needs Callable<T> and a `throws Exception` on retry. */ public class RetryJava { // A fake recipe website that times out a few times, then answers. static final class FlakySite { private int failuresLeft; int calls = 0; FlakySite(int failuresLeft) { this.failuresLeft = failuresLeft; } String fetch(String recipe) { calls++; if (failuresLeft-- > 0) throw new IllegalStateException("site timeout on call " + calls); return "page:" + recipe; } } // A higher-order method: the loop is written once, and the work comes in as a function. static <T> T retry(int times, Supplier<T> block) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int attempt = 1; attempt <= times; attempt++) { try { return block.get(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; System.out.println(" attempt " + attempt + " failed: " + e.getMessage()); } } throw new IllegalStateException("gave up after " + times + " attempts", last); } // Another one: run any block, report how long it took, hand back its result unchanged. static <T> T timed(String label, Supplier<T> block) { long start = System.nanoTime(); try { return block.get(); } finally { System.out.printf(" %s took %.2f ms%n", label, (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e6); } } public static void main(String[] args) { FlakySite site = new FlakySite(2); String page = timed("fetch with retry", () -> retry(3, () -> site.fetch("pancakes"))); System.out.println("result: " + page + " after " + site.calls + " calls"); FlakySite down = new FlakySite(5); try { retry(3, () -> down.fetch("waffles")); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("result: " + e.getMessage() + " (last cause: " + e.getCause().getMessage() + ")"); } } }

try.expect: The first half takes three calls: two timeouts, then page:pancakes. The second gives up after three: gave up after 3 attempts (last cause: site timeout on call 3). timed prints its line even when the block throws, because the print is in a finally. With retry(1), the program stops with IllegalStateException: gave up after 1 attempts, a message that never expected to be used with one attempt. retry never changed in any of these runs; only the function you handed it did.

sections.h: Handing back a function: set up the converter once
sections.html:
Higher-order works in the other direction too. A function can build another function and hand it back.

Here's a kitchen problem that needs it. Some recipes measure in millilitres, with a jug, but your scale wants grams. A litre of honey weighs roughly 1,420 g, and a litre of loosely spooned flour roughly 530 g. So the grams depend on two things: which ingredient, and how many millilitres. A plain function grams(ingredient, ml) takes both at once. This one takes the ingredient and returns a function that waits for the millilitres:

Java
static Function<Integer, Integer> gramsFor(String ingredient) {
    int perLitre = WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.get(ingredient);       // looked up once
    return ml -> ml * perLitre / 1_000;
}

Function<Integer, Integer> honey = gramsFor("honey");
honey.apply(250);                                          // 355
Kotlin
fun gramsFor(ingredient: String): (Int) -> Int {
    val perLitre = WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.getValue(ingredient)    // looked up once
    return { ml -> ml * perLitre / 1_000 }
}

val honey = gramsFor("honey")
honey(250)                                                 // 355

Fixing some of a function's arguments and getting back a function of the rest is called partial application. In the kitchen, it's a card with one blank already filled in: "honey", so only the amount is left to write.

It pays off when the first argument is known early and the second arrives many times. Baking a honey cake, you know the ingredient once and measure many times. gramsFor looks the weight up once, and the closure it returns (lesson 2 of this track) keeps only the number it needs.

It also moves failure to the right moment. An unknown ingredient fails when you build the function, not halfway through the cake. Ask for gramsFor("sand") and you hear about it at once, before a single gram is weighed.

Currying takes the same idea all the way: every function takes exactly one argument and returns a function for the next. A curried converter has the type (String) -> (Int) -> Int. The arrows group to the right, so read it as (String) -> ((Int) -> Int).

Java
Function<String, Function<Integer, Integer>> curriedGrams = ingredient -> ml -> grams(ingredient, ml);
curriedGrams.apply("flour").apply(500);                    // 265
Kotlin
val curriedGrams: (String) -> (Int) -> Int = { ingredient -> { ml -> grams(ingredient, ml) } }
curriedGrams("flour")(500)                                 // 265

Some languages, Haskell for one, curry every function. In Kotlin, don't. The signatures get hard to read and the IDE hints get noisy. And Kotlin already covers what currying is for: a lambda that fixes one argument ({ ml: Int -> grams("milk", ml) }), default and named arguments, and bound references like oven::adjust from the last lesson.

Return a function when you mean "set up now, run many times". That's the case that earns its keep.

One card at a time is useful. Clipping several cards together is where real recipes come from.

try.title: When does a bad ingredient fail?
steps: Run GramsFor (or GramsForJava) and check one number: 250 ml of honey at 1,420 g a litre is 355 g.
Add val broken = gramsFor("sand") as the first line of main, without calling broken. Predict whether the program fails, and where.

Move the lookup into the returned lambda: return { ml -> ml * WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.getValue(ingredient) / 1_000 } (Java: WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.get(ingredient) inside the lambda). Run again. Now when does it fail?

code.title: GramsFor.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo // Roughly what one litre weighs, in grams. The jug measures millilitres; the scale wants grams. val WEIGHT_PER_LITRE = mapOf("flour" to 530, "milk" to 1_030, "honey" to 1_420) // Both arguments at once. fun grams(ingredient: String, ml: Int): Int = ml * WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.getValue(ingredient) / 1_000 // Partial application: fix the ingredient now, get back a function of the volume. fun gramsFor(ingredient: String): (Int) -> Int { val perLitre = WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.getValue(ingredient) // looked up once, right here return { ml -> ml * perLitre / 1_000 } } // Currying by hand: take one argument, return a function that takes the next one. val curriedGrams: (String) -> (Int) -> Int = { ingredient -> { ml -> grams(ingredient, ml) } } fun main() { val honey = gramsFor("honey") println("gramsFor(\"honey\")(250) = ${honey(250)}") println("curriedGrams(\"flour\")(500) = ${curriedGrams("flour")(500)}") // Kotlin idioms that usually read better than a curried signature: val milkGrams = { ml: Int -> grams("milk", ml) } // a lambda that fixes one argument println("lambda that fixes milk = ${milkGrams(250)}") println("named arguments = ${grams(ml = 250, ingredient = "honey")}") val jugs = listOf(100, 250, 1_000) println("jugs.map(honey) = ${jugs.map(honey)}") }

alt.title: GramsForJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.Function; /** Java twin of GramsFor.kt. Partial application and currying with java.util.function.Function. */ public class GramsForJava { // Roughly what one litre weighs, in grams. The jug measures millilitres; the scale wants grams. static final Map<String, Integer> WEIGHT_PER_LITRE = Map.of("flour", 530, "milk", 1_030, "honey", 1_420); // Both arguments at once. static int grams(String ingredient, int ml) { return ml * WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.get(ingredient) / 1_000; } // Partial application: fix the ingredient now, get back a function of the volume. static Function<Integer, Integer> gramsFor(String ingredient) { int perLitre = WEIGHT_PER_LITRE.get(ingredient); // looked up once, right here return ml -> ml * perLitre / 1_000; } // Currying by hand: the type says it all. static final Function<String, Function<Integer, Integer>> CURRIED_GRAMS = ingredient -> ml -> grams(ingredient, ml); public static void main(String[] args) { Function<Integer, Integer> honey = gramsFor("honey"); System.out.println("gramsFor(\"honey\").apply(250) = " + honey.apply(250)); System.out.println("CURRIED_GRAMS.apply(\"flour\").apply(500) = " + CURRIED_GRAMS.apply("flour").apply(500)); // A lambda that fixes one argument. (Java has no named arguments.) Function<Integer, Integer> milkGrams = ml -> grams("milk", ml); System.out.println("lambda that fixes milk = " + milkGrams.apply(250)); List<Integer> jugs = List.of(100, 250, 1_000); System.out.println("jugs.stream().map(honey) = " + jugs.stream().map(honey).toList()); } }

try.expect: With the lookup outside the lambda, gramsFor("sand") fails right away: Kotlin throws NoSuchElementException: Key sand is missing in the map., and Java throws a NullPointerException when it unboxes the missing weight. With the lookup inside the lambda, gramsFor("sand") succeeds and returns a function that fails on its first call, which could be much later. Same code, different moment of failure. You want the first one.

sections.h: Clipping small functions together: composition, where order matters
sections.html:
Adjustments to a recipe come in small pieces. Scale it from four people to six. Use 10 % less sugar, as plenty of cooks do. Never use more than the 250 g left in the bag. Each piece is an (Int) -> Int on grams. The amount you actually weigh out is some of those pieces run one after another, and every cook has a different set.

Running one function on the result of another is called composition. Java's Function interface has it built in, as two default methods, andThen and compose:

Java
Function<Integer, Integer> sugar = FOR_SIX_GUESTS.andThen(TEN_PERCENT_LESS).andThen(AT_MOST_THE_BAG);
sugar.apply(200);                                          // 250
Kotlin
infix fun <A, B, C> ((A) -> B).andThen(next: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> next(this(a)) }

val sugar = forSixGuests andThen tenPercentLess andThen atMostTheBag
sugar(200)                                                 // 250

Kotlin's standard library has no andThen or compose for function types. Without the one-line extension above, forSixGuests andThen tenPercentLess fails with unresolved reference 'andThen' on receiver of type '(Int) -> Int'. Arrow, the best-known functional library for Kotlin, ships andThen, compose and curried in a separate arrow-functions module. This track's lab doesn't depend on it.

One line is all you need, and writing it shows there's no magic: this is the first function, this(a) calls it, and next gets the result. infix lets you write it without dots and parentheses, so the steps read left to right in the order they run. compose is the same with the arguments swapped, (g compose f)(x) == g(f(x)), as mathematicians write it. Pick one and stay with it. andThen matches the way people read.

Two things about composition matter in practice. The first is that the order is part of the result. The demo runs the same three steps both ways:

recipe says 100 g -> 135 g   (cap first: 135 g)
recipe says 200 g -> 250 g   (cap first: 270 g)

For 100 g the cap never bites, so the order doesn't show. For 200 g, scaling gives 300 g, 10 % less gives 270 g, and the cap brings it down to the 250 g you have. Cap first, and you check the bag before you've scaled: the recipe then asks for 270 g of sugar you don't own. It's the same with mixing, baking and icing. Ice before you bake and you still get something, just not a cake.

The second is that a list of steps folds into one function, starting from the function that returns its input unchanged:

Java
Function<Integer, Integer> fromList = steps.stream()
        .reduce(Function.identity(), (acc, step) -> acc.andThen(step));
Kotlin
val fromList = steps.fold({ x: Int -> x }) { acc, step -> acc andThen step }

That's how saved settings become code. Read a cook's adjustments when the app starts, turn each one into a function, fold them into one (Int) -> Int, and call it for every ingredient. Every piece stays small, pure and testable on its own. (Lesson 4 of this track covers fold properly.)

The order of the steps is part of the function. Test them in the order you'll run them.

Composition builds new functions out of old ones. The next higher-order function improves a function without changing a single one of its answers.

try.title: Compose, reorder, extend
steps: Run Compose (or ComposeJava). Predict both amounts for 100 g and for 200 g before you look.
Delete the andThen extension at the top of Compose.kt and run again. Read the error, then put the line back.
Add a fourth step, val roundToTen: (Int) -> Int = { it / 10 * 10 }, at the end of steps, and print fromList(130). Predict it first.

code.title: Compose.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo // The stdlib has no andThen for function types, so here it is. Remove it and the file stops compiling. infix fun <A, B, C> ((A) -> B).andThen(next: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> next(this(a)) } val forSixGuests: (Int) -> Int = { it * 6 / 4 } // the recipe serves four val tenPercentLess: (Int) -> Int = { it * 90 / 100 } // less sugar, rounded down val atMostTheBag: (Int) -> Int = { minOf(it, 250) } // only 250 g left in the bag fun main() { val sugar = forSixGuests andThen tenPercentLess andThen atMostTheBag val capFirst = atMostTheBag andThen forSixGuests andThen tenPercentLess for (grams in listOf(100, 200)) { println("recipe says $grams g -> ${sugar(grams)} g (cap first: ${capFirst(grams)} g)") } // Built from a list, the way a saved set of adjustments would build it. val steps = listOf(forSixGuests, tenPercentLess, atMostTheBag) val fromList = steps.fold({ x: Int -> x }) { acc, step -> acc andThen step } println("fromList(200) = ${fromList(200)}") }

alt.title: ComposeJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.function.Function; /** Java twin of Compose.kt. java.util.function.Function has andThen and compose built in, as default methods. */ public class ComposeJava { static final Function<Integer, Integer> FOR_SIX_GUESTS = g -> g * 6 / 4; // the recipe serves four static final Function<Integer, Integer> TEN_PERCENT_LESS = g -> g * 90 / 100; // less sugar, rounded down static final Function<Integer, Integer> AT_MOST_THE_BAG = g -> Math.min(g, 250); // only 250 g left in the bag public static void main(String[] args) { Function<Integer, Integer> sugar = FOR_SIX_GUESTS.andThen(TEN_PERCENT_LESS).andThen(AT_MOST_THE_BAG); Function<Integer, Integer> capFirst = AT_MOST_THE_BAG.andThen(FOR_SIX_GUESTS).andThen(TEN_PERCENT_LESS); for (int grams : new int[] {100, 200}) { System.out.println("recipe says " + grams + " g -> " + sugar.apply(grams) + " g (cap first: " + capFirst.apply(grams) + " g)"); } // Built from a list, the way a saved set of adjustments would build it. List<Function<Integer, Integer>> steps = List.of(FOR_SIX_GUESTS, TEN_PERCENT_LESS, AT_MOST_THE_BAG); Function<Integer, Integer> fromList = steps.stream() .reduce(Function.identity(), (acc, step) -> acc.andThen(step)); System.out.println("fromList(200) = " + fromList.apply(200)); } }

try.expect: 100 g gives 135 g both ways, because the cap never bites. 200 g gives 250 g with the cap last and 270 g with the cap first. Without the extension, Kotlin reports unresolved reference 'andThen' on receiver of type '(Int) -> Int'. The Java version has nothing to delete: andThen is a default method on Function. With roundToTen, fromList(130) goes 195, then 175, then 175 again (under the cap), then 170.

sections.h: memoize: a function that remembers its answers, and when that lies
sections.html:
A higher-order function can also take a function and return an improved version of it. memoize returns a function that gives the same answers as the original but works each one out only once. Picture the friend writing the answer on the back of the card the first time, and reading it off after that.

Java
static <A, R> Function<A, R> memoize(Function<A, R> f) {
    Map<A, R> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    return a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a, f);
}

Function<String, Integer> kcal = memoize(Foods::kcalPer100g);
Kotlin
fun <A : Any, R : Any> memoize(f: (A) -> R): (A) -> R {
    val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<A, R>()
    return { a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a) { f(it) } }
}

val kcal = memoize(::kcalPer100g)

Everything from the last lesson is in those few lines. memoize takes a function and returns one. The returned lambda is a closure over cache, so each memoized function gets its own map that nobody else can reach.

It's safe on many threads because the captured state is a ConcurrentHashMap, a map built to be shared by threads, held in a val rather than a var. computeIfAbsent runs f at most once per key, even when two threads ask for the same key at the same moment, as the concurrent collections lesson showed. The A : Any, R : Any bounds are there because ConcurrentHashMap can't store null.

The demo's food table is slow on purpose, 50 ms a lookup, like a long table searched from the top every time. Five calls for oats and honey:

[389, 304, 389, 389, 304]
lookups: 2 for 5 calls, 129 ms

Two lookups instead of five, and the same answers.

Memoizing is only correct for pure functions. Referential transparency, from lesson 1, says a pure call can be replaced by its value, and a cache does exactly that replacement for you. Memoize something impure and you get stale answers. The demo also memoizes eggsIn("fridge"), which reads how many eggs are left:

eggs in the fridge now:        6
eggs after someone's omelette: 6   (really: 2)

The memo says six. The fridge holds two, and the memo will keep saying six until the program restarts. Here the friend picture breaks: a real cook can open the fridge and look, but a memo has no way to tell that its answer went stale.

Calories per 100 g of oats from a fixed table is a good fit. How many eggs are left, today's price of butter, or anything you read from a file or a database is not.

Memoize only pure functions. A saved answer is right only if the function would have given it again.

Two practical limits. The cache never forgets, so only memoize over a small, known set of keys (ingredients, units, recipe names), never over something that keeps growing, like timestamps. When you need expiry or a size limit, use a real cache library such as Caffeine, which is the same idea plus eviction, throwing old entries out. And the function you pass to computeIfAbsent must not change the same map, so this memoize can't wrap a recursive function that calls its own memoized version.

Each of these higher-order functions takes a lambda, and a lambda is an object. So what do all those objects cost?

try.title: A memo that helps, and one that lies
steps: Run Memoize (or MemoizeJava). Predict the number of lookups for the five foods, and roughly how long they take (each real lookup sleeps 50 ms).
Replace memoize(::kcalPer100g) with plain ::kcalPer100g and run again.
Explain the last line of the output to yourself before you read the expected result. Why is the memoized egg count wrong?

code.title: Memoize.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap // A higher-order function that returns a function: same answers as f, but each one computed once. fun <A : Any, R : Any> memoize(f: (A) -> R): (A) -> R { val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<A, R>() // captured: one cache per memoized function return { a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a) { f(it) } } } // Pure but slow: imagine it searches a long food table on every call. var tableLookups = 0 fun kcalPer100g(food: String): Int { tableLookups++ Thread.sleep(50) return if (food == "oats") 389 else 304 } // Impure: the number of eggs changes whenever someone cooks. var fridgeEggs = 6 fun eggsIn(place: String): Int = if (place == "fridge") fridgeEggs else 0 fun main() { val kcal = memoize(::kcalPer100g) val foods = listOf("oats", "honey", "oats", "oats", "honey") val start = System.nanoTime() println(foods.map(kcal)) println("lookups: $tableLookups for ${foods.size} calls, %d ms".format((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000)) val eggs = memoize(::eggsIn) println("eggs in the fridge now: ${eggs("fridge")}") fridgeEggs = 2 // someone makes an omelette println("eggs after someone's omelette: ${eggs("fridge")} (really: ${eggsIn("fridge")})") }

alt.title: MemoizeJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.function.Function; /** Java twin of Memoize.kt. */ public class MemoizeJava { // A higher-order method that returns a function: same answers as f, but each one computed once. static <A, R> Function<A, R> memoize(Function<A, R> f) { Map<A, R> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // captured: one cache per memoized function return a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a, f); } // Pure but slow: imagine it searches a long food table on every call. static int tableLookups = 0; static int kcalPer100g(String food) { tableLookups++; try { Thread.sleep(50); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } return food.equals("oats") ? 389 : 304; } // Impure: the number of eggs changes whenever someone cooks. static int fridgeEggs = 6; static int eggsIn(String place) { return place.equals("fridge") ? fridgeEggs : 0; } public static void main(String[] args) { Function<String, Integer> kcal = memoize(MemoizeJava::kcalPer100g); List<String> foods = List.of("oats", "honey", "oats", "oats", "honey"); long start = System.nanoTime(); System.out.println(foods.stream().map(kcal).toList()); System.out.printf("lookups: %d for %d calls, %d ms%n", tableLookups, foods.size(), (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000); Function<String, Integer> eggs = memoize(MemoizeJava::eggsIn); System.out.println("eggs in the fridge now: " + eggs.apply("fridge")); fridgeEggs = 2; // someone makes an omelette System.out.println("eggs after someone's omelette: " + eggs.apply("fridge") + " (really: " + eggsIn("fridge") + ")"); } }

try.expect: Memoized: 2 lookups for 5 calls, a little over 100 ms. Without memoize: 5 lookups, about 250 ms, and the same answers. The egg line prints 6 after the fridge dropped to 2. eggsIn reads a mutable global, so it is impure, and the memo froze its first answer. A cache is only invisible when the function it wraps is pure.

sections.h: inline: why map and filter create no lambdas
sections.html:
Every lambda you pass to retry or memoize is an object (lesson 2), and a var it changes becomes a Ref box. So you might expect recipes.filter { ... }.map { ... } to create two lambda objects on every call. It creates none, because filter, map, forEach, fold, sumOf and almost every other collection function on Iterable are declared inline.

When you call an inline function, the compiler doesn't emit a call. It copies the function's body into the call site, and the lambda's body with it. The lambda never exists as an object.

Java
// Java has no inline functions. The method reference is a lambda object
// (shared, since it captures nothing), and only the JIT may inline it at runtime.
long total = grams.stream().mapToLong(Long::longValue).sum();
Kotlin
inline fun <T> measuredInline(block: () -> T): T {
    val start = System.nanoTime()
    val result = block()
    lastNanos = System.nanoTime() - start
    return result
}

var total = 0L
measuredInline { grams.forEach { total += it } }   // becomes a plain loop; total stays a local

The InlineCost demo compiles two versions of the same code and adds up 500 g, 250 g and 1,000 g, the flour, sugar and milk for one cake. With a non-inline measured, the bytecode (the instructions the JVM actually runs) has new Ref$LongRef, a box for total. It also has an invokedynamic, the instruction that creates the lambda object, and a call through Function0.invoke.

With measuredInline it has none of them: the System.nanoTime() calls, the iterator loop and an ladd on a local variable are pasted straight into totalInlined. (ladd is the bytecode instruction that adds two long values.) The JIT compiler, the part of the JVM that turns busy code into machine code while the program runs, may inline Java's lambda later. Kotlin's inline does it before the program ever starts.

That's also why return inside repeat worked in retry. After inlining, the lambda body is part of retry, so return leaves retry. This is called a non-local return, and it's only allowed when the lambda is inlined.

Inline a small higher-order function that calls its lambda right away. Leave the rest alone.

So mark your own small higher-order functions inline when they take a lambda and call it straight away, as measuredInline and retry do. Don't mark everything inline. The body is copied into every call site, so a big inline function bloats the code. And a lambda you keep for later, like the f that memoize stores in its closure, can't be inlined: the compiler needs a real object to keep. The Advanced Kotlin track, later in this part of the course, has a whole lesson on inline, noinline, crossinline and non-local returns.

inline removes the lambda objects, not the work. Each filter or map on a list still builds a whole new list, and that's the cost the next lesson puts on the table.

try.title: Find the missing lambda in the bytecode
steps: Run InlineCost. Both totals print 1750. (Java has no inline functions, so this demo has no Java twin.)

From labs/, run javap -c -p functional/build/classes/kotlin/demo/workbench/functional/l03/demo/InlineCostKt.class. Compare totalWithLambda with totalInlined: look for Ref$LongRef, invokedynamic and System.nanoTime.
Predict what changes in totalInlined if you delete the word inline from measuredInline. Then try it.

code.title: InlineCost.kt
code.html: package workbench.functional.l03.demo var lastNanos = 0L // Not inline: the lambda becomes an object, and a var it changes becomes a Ref box. fun <T> measured(block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() val result = block() lastNanos = System.nanoTime() - start return result } // Inline: the compiler pastes this body, and the lambda's body, into every caller. inline fun <T> measuredInline(block: () -> T): T { val start = System.nanoTime() val result = block() lastNanos = System.nanoTime() - start return result } fun totalWithLambda(grams: List<Long>): Long { var total = 0L measured { for (g in grams) total += g } return total } fun totalInlined(grams: List<Long>): Long { var total = 0L measuredInline { grams.forEach { total += it } } return total } fun main() { val grams = listOf(500L, 250L, 1_000L) // flour, sugar and milk for one cake println("with a lambda object: ${totalWithLambda(grams)}") println("inlined: ${totalInlined(grams)}") }

try.expect: totalWithLambda has new kotlin/jvm/internal/Ref$LongRef, an invokedynamic that makes a Function0, and a call to measured. totalInlined has none of them: it calls System.nanoTime itself and adds into a local with ladd. Without inline, totalInlined looks like totalWithLambda: a Ref$LongRef, an invokedynamic and a call to measuredInline. measuredInline also exists as an ordinary method in the class, for callers such as Java code that can't inline it.

compare.title: Functions in, functions out, functions combined

java.title: Kitchen.java
java.html: import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap; import java.util.function.Function; import java.util.function.Supplier; final class Kitchen { // functions in static <T> T retry(int times, Supplier<T> block) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) { try { return block.get(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; } } throw new IllegalStateException("gave up after " + times + " attempts", last); } // functions out: partial application static Function<Integer, Integer> gramsFor(int perLitre) { return ml -> ml * perLitre / 1_000; } // composition is built into Function static Function<Integer, Integer> sugarToWeigh(int perLitre) { return gramsFor(perLitre).andThen(g -> g * 90 / 100).andThen(g -> Math.min(g, 250)); } static <A, R> Function<A, R> memoize(Function<A, R> f) { Map<A, R> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); return a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a, f); } }

kotlin.title: Kitchen.kt
kotlin.html: import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap // functions in; inline, so the lambda is pasted into the caller inline fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: () -> T): T { var last: Exception? = null repeat(times) { try { return block() } catch (e: Exception) { last = e } } throw IllegalStateException("gave up after $times attempts", last) } // functions out: partial application fun gramsFor(perLitre: Int): (Int) -> Int = { ml -> ml * perLitre / 1_000 } // composition is not in the stdlib: one line of your own infix fun <A, B, C> ((A) -> B).andThen(next: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> next(this(a)) } fun sugarToWeigh(perLitre: Int): (Int) -> Int = gramsFor(perLitre) andThen { g -> g * 90 / 100 } andThen { g -> minOf(g, 250) } fun <A : Any, R : Any> memoize(f: (A) -> R): (A) -> R { val cache = ConcurrentHashMap<A, R>() return { a -> cache.computeIfAbsent(a) { f(it) } } }

compare.note: Both languages make the same three moves: functions in, functions out, functions combined. The differences are in the plumbing. Java's Function comes with andThen and compose, and Kotlin's function types don't, so you write the extension yourself or use Arrow's arrow-functions module. Java needs a different interface per shape (Supplier, Function, Callable once checked exceptions appear), while Kotlin uses () -> T and (A) -> R everywhere. And Kotlin can declare a higher-order function inline, so the lambda passed to retry is pasted into the caller and never allocated. Java leaves that to the JIT, which may or may not inline at runtime.

worked.title: Turn a cook's saved adjustments into one function

steps.say: A cook's adjustments are saved as rows: a kind of adjustment and a number. We want one (Int) -> Int per ingredient, built once when the app starts and called for every measurement. The base step is the jug-to-scale converter, gramsFor(ingredient), from the second section.
steps.code: data class AdjustmentRow(val kind: String, val value: Int) val myRows = listOf( AdjustmentRow("less", 10), // 10 % less AdjustmentRow("atLeast", 50), // at least 50 g AdjustmentRow("atMost", 300), // at most 300 g )

alt.html: record AdjustmentRow(String kind, int value) {} List<AdjustmentRow> myRows = List.of( new AdjustmentRow("less", 10), // 10 % less new AdjustmentRow("atLeast", 50), // at least 50 g new AdjustmentRow("atMost", 300)); // at most 300 g

steps.say: 1. Turn each row into a function with a when expression. Each branch returns a function, and nothing is computed yet. An unknown kind is a bug in the saved settings, so it throws here.
steps.code: fun toAdjust(row: AdjustmentRow): (Int) -> Int = when (row.kind) { "add" -> { g -> g + row.value } "less" -> { g -> g * (100 - row.value) / 100 } "atLeast" -> { g -> maxOf(g, row.value) } "atMost" -> { g -> minOf(g, row.value) } else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown adjustment ${row.kind}") }

alt.html: static Function<Integer, Integer> toAdjust(AdjustmentRow row) { return switch (row.kind()) { case "add" -> g -> g + row.value(); case "less" -> g -> g * (100 - row.value()) / 100; case "atLeast" -> g -> Math.max(g, row.value()); case "atMost" -> g -> Math.min(g, row.value()); default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown adjustment " + row.kind()); }; }

steps.say: 1. Fold the adjustments onto the ingredient's converter. Self-check: when does a row with an unknown kind fail, at startup or at the first measurement? (At startup: toAdjust runs inside map, while the function is being built.)
steps.code: fun measure(ingredient: String, rows: List<AdjustmentRow>): (Int) -> Int = rows.map(::toAdjust) // 1. rows to functions .fold(gramsFor(ingredient)) { acc, f -> acc andThen f } // 2. one function, converter first

alt.html: static Function<Integer, Integer> measure(String ingredient, List<AdjustmentRow> rows) { return rows.stream() .map(Kitchen::toAdjust) // 1. rows to functions .reduce(gramsFor(ingredient), Function::andThen); // 2. one function, converter first }

steps.say: 1. Build once per ingredient, call per measurement. Each measurement now costs four small calls and no lookups, and every adjustment can be tested on its own with plain numbers.
steps.code: val sugar = measure("sugar", myRows) sugar(500) // 425 -> 382 -> 382 -> 300 sugar(50) // 42 -> 37 -> 50 -> 50

alt.html: Function<Integer, Integer> sugar = measure("sugar", myRows); sugar.apply(500); // 425 -> 382 -> 382 -> 300 sugar.apply(50); // 42 -> 37 -> 50 -> 50

lab.title: Compose a measuring pipeline, and memoize a slow lookup
steps: Run the tests. All ten fail with NotImplementedError. Read the four finished building blocks at the top of Pipeline.kt (add, percentLess, atMost, atLeast): each one is a function that returns a function.
Write andThen and compose. Each body is one lambda.
Write pipeline with fold, starting from { x: T -> x }. An empty list must give back that identity function.
Write gramsFor. Do the lookup outside the lambda you return, and throw IllegalArgumentException("unknown ingredient $ingredient") for an ingredient that isn't in GRAMS_PER_LITRE.
Write weighOut from gramsFor, andThen and pipeline. Then write curried.
Write memoize in Memo.kt. Run the tests until all ten pass.
hints: andThen is { a -> next(this(a)) }. Inside an extension on a function type, this is the function, and this(a) calls it.
requireNotNull(GRAMS_PER_LITRE[ingredient]) { "unknown ingredient $ingredient" } returns the weight, or throws IllegalArgumentException with that message.

ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent(key) { f(it) } calls f only when the key is missing. A HashMap with getOrPut also passes these tests, but it isn't safe once several threads share the memoized function.

drill.title: Write retry and andThen from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write an inline function retry(times, block) that calls block until it returns, at most times times, and then throws IllegalStateException with the last failure as its cause. Write andThen for function types. Use both: retry a call that fetches a recipe's sugar in grams from a website, then run the grams through { it * 90 / 100 } andThen { minOf(it, 250) }. Then write the Java version of both functions.

answer.html: inline fun <T> retry(times: Int, block: () -> T): T { var last: Exception? = null repeat(times) { try { return block() } catch (e: Exception) { last = e } // non-local return: repeat is inline } throw IllegalStateException("gave up after $times attempts", last) } infix fun <A, B, C> ((A) -> B).andThen(next: (B) -> C): (A) -> C = { a -> next(this(a)) } val adjust: (Int) -> Int = { g: Int -> g * 90 / 100 } andThen { g -> minOf(g, 250) } val sugar = adjust(retry(3) { site.sugarGrams("pancakes") })

alt.html: static <T> T retry(int times, Supplier<T> block) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) { try { return block.get(); } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; } } throw new IllegalStateException("gave up after " + times + " attempts", last); } // andThen is already a default method on java.util.function.Function Function<Integer, Integer> lessSugar = g -> g * 90 / 100; Function<Integer, Integer> adjust = lessSugar.andThen(g -> Math.min(g, 250)); int sugar = adjust.apply(retry(3, () -> site.sugarGrams("pancakes")));

recap: A higher-order function takes a function, returns one, or both. It keeps the shape of a computation (retry, time, remember) apart from the work inside it.
Trailing lambdas make higher-order calls read like built-ins: retry(3) { site.fetch("pancakes") }.
Returning a function gives you partial application: gramsFor(ingredient) looks the weight up once and returns an (Int) -> Int. Prefer that, or a plain lambda, to curried signatures.
Kotlin's stdlib has no andThen or compose for function types; write the one-line infix extension (Java's Function has both). Order matters, and a list of steps folds into one function.
Memoize only pure functions, over a small set of keys. A memoized impure function returns stale answers until restart, and it can't tell.

inline pastes a function and its lambda into the call site: no lambda object, no Ref box, and return leaves the enclosing function. Its limit: each map or filter on a list still builds a whole new list.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why recipes.filter { it.vegan }.map { it.name } creates no lambda objects, while their own fun <T> timed(block: () -> T): T does. Explain it in your own words, and say what you'd change in timed.
explain.answer: A lambda is normally an object: a function value that something has to create, and if it changes a captured var, that var moves into a Ref box. filter and map on lists are declared inline, so the compiler never calls them. It copies their loops into my method and pastes my lambda bodies into those loops, and no lambda object ever exists. timed isn't inline, so its block has to be a real object passed to a real call. Since timed only calls block once, right away, I'd mark it inline. Then the timing code and the block are pasted into each caller, with no allocation and no Ref box. I wouldn't do that for a function that stores its lambda, like memoize, because a stored lambda has to be an object.

deeper.html:
Kotlin gives you partial application in a few forms besides returning a lambda. A bound reference fixes the receiver, which is often all you need:

Java
final class Oven {
    private final int extraMinutes;
    Oven(int extraMinutes) { this.extraMinutes = extraMinutes; }
    int adjust(int minutes) { return minutes + extraMinutes; }
}

Oven myOven = new Oven(5);
Function<Integer, Integer> bake = myOven::adjust;    // a bound method reference
List.of(20, 35).stream().map(bake).toList();          // [25, 40]
Kotlin
class Oven(private val extraMinutes: Int) {
    fun adjust(minutes: Int): Int = minutes + extraMinutes
}

val myOven = Oven(extraMinutes = 5)               // this oven runs a little cold
val bake: (Int) -> Int = myOven::adjust           // a bound reference: the receiver is fixed
listOf(20, 35).map(bake)                          // [25, 40]

This is the strategy pattern with the ceremony removed: an object with one behaviour, passed around as a function. Remember lesson 2's detail, though: in Kotlin 2.4.21 a bound reference compiles to a small class and allocates one object each time the expression runs.

Arrow 2.3.0 puts its function utilities in the io.arrow-kt:arrow-functions artifact, separate from arrow-core. Its jar contains andThen and compose, curried and uncurried with overloads up to 22 parameters, partially1 and its siblings, and memoize. If your codebase already uses Arrow, use those rather than your own. If it doesn't, the one-line versions in this lesson are not a reason to add a dependency.

One more look at inline and return. Inside an inline higher-order function's lambda, a bare return leaves the enclosing function, and return@forEach (or any label) leaves only the lambda, acting like continue. Java developers moving to Kotlin trip on this in forEach, because a return in a Java Stream.forEach lambda only ends that one call. The Advanced Kotlin track's inline lesson goes through noinline and crossinline, the two modifiers that control which lambdas get pasted and where return may go.
